paragraphs.heading: The crust's main ingredient
paragraphs.text: Silicate minerals are rock-forming minerals built out of silicate groups. No other class of minerals is as large or as important. Together they account for roughly 90 percent of Earth's crust.

paragraphs.heading: How a silicate is put together
paragraphs.text: A silicate mineral is generally an inorganic compound made of subunits with the formula [SiO₂₊ₙ]²ⁿ⁻. In most silicate minerals the silicon is tetrahedral, which here means it is surrounded by four oxides. The silicate subunits are drawn as anions, and metal cations, written Mˣ⁺, balance their charges. Typical cations are Mg²⁺, Fe²⁺ and Na⁺. Calling the silicates anions is a simplification, though. The Si-O-M links that tie the silicates to the metals are strong, polar-covalent bonds.

paragraphs.heading: Where the color comes from
paragraphs.text: The silicate anions themselves are always colorless. Crushed to a fine powder, they are white. The colors of silicate minerals come from the metal component instead, and that metal is commonly iron.

paragraphs.heading: Made and remade over time
paragraphs.text: Earth holds a wide variety of silicate minerals, and they turn up in an even wider range of combinations. This is the result of processes that have been forming and reworking the crust for billions of years. Among them are weathering, metamorphism, crystallization, partial melting, fractionation and diagenesis.

paragraphs.heading: Living things join in
paragraphs.text: Living organisms also contribute to this geologic cycle. Diatoms, a type of plankton, are one example. They take silica out of seawater and use it to build their exoskeletons, which are called frustules. When diatoms die, their frustules become a major part of deep ocean sediment. They are also a major part of a material called diatomaceous earth.

paragraphs.heading: Silica and a sorting disagreement
paragraphs.text: Silica has the formula SiO₂, and it occurs in nature as the mineral quartz. In mineralogy, the crystalline forms of silica are usually considered to be tectosilicates. One system, the Dana classification, files them that way. Another, the Nickel–Strunz classification, puts them among the oxide minerals instead. Tectosilicates can take on extra cations only if an atom of lower valence, such as aluminum, takes the place of some of their silicon, and swapping aluminum in for silicon is common.
